Capability detection npx ffmpeg-skill doctor # human-readable npx ffmpeg-skill doctor --json # available / missing / missing_optional / unknown / detection / errors / tools / gpu_encoders / ffmpeg_security doctor reads ffmpeg -encoders, -decoders, -filters and -bsfs and resolves every capability the contract declares against this machine's build. Three states per capability: available, missing, unknown. Exit 0 when everything required is available, 1 when something required is missing, 2 when nothing is proven missing but a required capability is unknown. With detection on (the default), contract --json carries the same lists under capabilities. doctor also reports fonts: the default drawtext family, and fonts.scripts — one available/missing/unknown per writing system (ja, zh, ko, ar, he, hi, bn, ta, th, lo, ru, el, latin) with the file it would use — so "can this machine render Korean captions" is answered before the job, not after. doctor --json's tools field folds that down to one answer per tool — {"caption": {"usable": "no", "missing": ["filter:subtitles"], "fix": "..."}, ...} — so "is doctor overall ok" and "can I run caption.py on this machine" are answered separately: a plain Homebrew ffmpeg is ok for tools that don't need subtitles/drawtext/zscale, while caption's own usable is "no". doctor --json's gpu_encoders reports which GPU-backed encoders (nvenc, videotoolbox, qsv, vaapi, amf) this ffmpeg build was compiled with — read from -encoders alone, so it proves the capability shipped, not that the GPU/driver on this machine will actually accept a job (that needs a real encode, which doctor's introspection never runs). It never affects ok or any tool's usable. The one GPU path a tool uses is Apple VideoToolbox, opt-in: --hw on every re-encoding tool (h264/hevc/prores on the GPU, AV1 stays on SVT-AV1), FFMPEG_SKILL_HW=1 to make it this machine's default for everything except export.py's delivery presets (those take --hw explicitly, or render.py --hw for a whole project). It runs only on Apple Silicon and never by default, except on a build with no libx264/libx265 (an LGPL ffmpeg that has only h264_videotoolbox/hevc_videotoolbox): there it is the only encoder, so every re-encoding tool and export.py's presets use it without --hw, the result says hw.source: "auto", and doctor lists the missing x264/x265 under covered_by instead of calling the tools unusable (--no-hw still asks for the CPU). It falls back to the CPU encoder — reported in the result's hw.fallback/hw.notes — only when VideoToolbox itself refuses a job (any other ffmpeg failure is reported as it happened, not retried); every result names the encoder that actually ran (batch.py, which encodes nothing itself: each results row), and a GPU encode adds a notes line that its quality is not CRF-equivalent. Measured on an M4 Max, 2–7× faster than x264/x265 medium; at matched SSIM (tests/bench_vt.py) 1.1–2.9× the bytes on SDR and 1.9–3.5× on HDR, which is why it is a flag and not the default (docs/design-decisions.md). doctor --json's hw says whether this machine can run it (platform_ok) and whether it is the default here (default_on). doctor also compares the FFmpeg version with a small, dated table of high-severity FFmpeg CVEs (doctor --json's ffmpeg_security; source ffmpeg.org/security.html, checked 2026-10-22). ffmpeg-skill does not ship FFmpeg, so a decoder bug in the build you have stays yours until you upgrade it. When the version is older than the first upstream release on its branch that carries a fix (today: CVE-2026-8461, the MagicYUV decoder heap write, fixed in 8.0.3, 8.1.2 and 9.0), doctor prints one warning: line on stderr with the update command and lists it under ffmpeg_security.warnings. It is advice, never a failure: ok, each tool's usable and the exit code do not change. A distribution package (Ubuntu 8.0.1-3ubuntu2, Debian +deb13u1) may carry the fix as a backport under the old version number, so the line says the build is older than the fix, not that it is vulnerable. A version it cannot read (a git snapshot such as N-12345-g…) gets no warning, and nothing is fetched: the table ships with the skill. Gotchas and best practices The short list for humans. The agent-facing version, with the reasoning, is the "Things that look right but are wrong" and "Gotchas" sections of SKILL.md. Variable frame rate (phone and screen recordings). probe.py flags it; every re-encoding tool conforms to a constant rate automatically. cut.py samples the frame timing before a copy and switches to frame-accurate mode when it is variable or too short to judge, because copy-cuts on VFR land on the wrong frame (--vfr-guard average restores 2.x's rule, re-encoding whenever the nominal and average rates differ; --vfr-guard off keeps the copy). Choose the rate yourself with fit.py input.mp4 --fps 30 when the measured average is odd. Lossless cuts snap to keyframes. A stream-copy cut can start up to one GOP earlier than asked. cut.py re-encodes when the snap exceeds 0.5 s (--tolerance changes the limit). For a strictly lossless file pass --tolerance -1 (plus --vfr-guard off on a variable-frame-rate source), and expect the cut to land on the nearest earlier keyframe; the JSON result lists them under nearest_keyframes. A --segments join can still be re-cut: open-GOP video, a later segment of B-frame .mp4/.mov video that starts between keyframes (start it on a keyframe, or write .mkv), or a join that fails its check. A single .mp4/.mov copy keeps its edit list by default (since 3.0.0), so the picture starts where asked: the keyframe's pre-roll is stored but hidden by an MP4 edit list, which a player that ignores edit lists shows (--no-edit-list starts the file at the keyframe instead). Frame-exact without re-encoding the whole cut (H.264). cut.py --smart re-encodes only from each cut point to the next keyframe and copies the GOPs between, matched to the source's profile, level, pixel format, B-frame depth and colour tags. It checks the result against the source (frame grid, copied packets, decoded frames). A source it cannot match (HEVC, 10-bit, interlaced, VFR, open GOPs) is re-encoded in full, and smart.reason says why. probe.py --keyframes-near T shows where the keyframes are. HDR stays HDR. When the probe reports HDR (HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision, BT.2020), the tools keep it rather than flatten it. Convert deliberately with color.py --to-sdr before H.264 deliverables or LUT work. export.py platform presets are SDR and warn on HDR input. Loudness targets. −14 LUFS / −1 dBTP for YouTube and social platforms (the loudness.py default), -I -16 --tp -1.5 for podcasts, -I -23 for broadcast. A clip measured at −40 LUFS or below is room tone, not content; raising it raises the noise. Check true peak as well as LUFS: check.py file --platform podcast measures both. Alpha is kept only when asked, and a lost alpha is not verified. The re-encoding tools write opaque H.264 by default. On a source whose alpha is used (ProRes 4444, QuickTime Animation, PNG, VP9 with alpha), color.py, graphics.py and overlay.py take --keep-alpha (ProRes 4444 by default, --alpha-codec qtrle|png|vp9, --alpha-mode straight|premultiplied) and read the alpha back; without it the result says verified: false with a failing alpha step, and --drop-alpha records that an opaque output is wanted. background.py --transparent makes the canvas to draw graphics on. Broadcast legal levels are measured, not assumed. check.py final.mxf --levels ebu-r103 (or bt709) counts every luma and chroma sample outside the legal range and FAILs when one frame has more than 1 % out (--levels-tolerance); the JSON levels adds min/max Y/U/V per --levels-window. color.py --correct --legalize ebu-r103 clamps after the 4:2:0 conversion and measures what the encode left: a lossy encoder can push a few samples around a clamped edge back out, so the result says how many. Frame changes first, text second. Captions and overlays burned before a crop or resize end up off-frame. Reframe, then caption. Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 discards 70 % of the width. fit.py --fit crop centres by default; pass --crop-x/--crop-y toward the subject, or pad with --fit pad --pad-fill blur. Look at the contact sheet before deciding. Phrase-aware caption breaking (1.16). caption.py/graphics.py --wrap phrase (the default) never breaks inside a word or on the wrong side of a hyphen, never leaves a lone digit, kana or punctuation pair on a line, prefers Japanese sentence ends and particles over a mid-word break, and never ends a line on an article or preposition. All four are penalties over break positions that already fit, so no line is widened and the line count never changes; --wrap measured restores 1.15's width-only wrap. The text itself is never rewritten or shortened. Since 1.16.1 a Thai run and a katakana word are never broken inside (Thai writes no space inside a phrase and there is no dictionary: the break goes where you put a space or |), and a line wider than the safe width is reported as overlong with the fix named. Caption size fitted to the cue (1.17, reachable from the templates since 1.17.1). At a platform caption size a line holds about six em, so an ordinary sentence needs four lines and --max-lines 2 used to cut it into consecutive cues — half the sentence arriving late. caption.py --fit-size (default auto) walks the size down until every cue fits, before laying the cues out, with a legibility floor of 4.5 % of the frame height (--min-size, default 13 ASS units). An explicit --size or a brand.json size is a statement about the look and is never overridden — which in 1.17.0 also silenced the fitter on every render.py --template run, since a template fills the size from the platform table; 1.17.1 marks that size as the default it is ("fit_size": "on" in the filled project), so the type shrinks and no cue is split. --fit-size off restores that earlier behaviour byte for byte, and the caption text is still never rewritten to make it fit. Beat-synced cuts (1.17). scenes.py --beats reports the measured grid — tempo, beat times, and a confidence built from how far the winning autocorrelation lag stands above the others and how many onsets land on it. cut.py --snap beats (and a "snap" block in a render.py project) moves in/out points to the nearest beat within --snap-tolerance — and only onto the grid points a measured onset actually marks, never onto the regular grid's continuation through a passage with no music in it. Below --min-confidence it refuses: a cut point may move to a measured beat and may not appear from one, so speech and ambience get an honest "no steady pulse here" instead of an invented grid. A music bed is measured as it is delivered, WAV/FLAC/MP3 with no picture; on a synthetic click track at 90 and 120 BPM every beat is within 1 ms (WAV/FLAC) or 9 ms (MP3) of its click, tests/test_analysis.py holds it to 20 ms. Filler words (1.17). silence.py --filler --words transcript.json removes "um" and "uh" through the same cut graph the silences use. Never without measured word timings — there is no heuristic that finds an "um" without them that would not also cut real speech — and like, tipo and cioè are deliberately not in the built-in lists, because a discourse marker is a content word. Built-in lists since 2.19: English, Japanese, Korean, Chinese, Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Russian and Turkish; any other language takes --filler-words FILE. Whisper stays optional: --transcribe with no engine installed refuses and names the five installs. Throughput (1.17). batch.py --jobs N runs several files at once, capped at min(N, cpu_count, 8) and sharing one --timeout budget rather than one per item; the per-item table keeps its order. render.py --cache DIR reuses stages whose inputs and arguments did not change, so swapping an export preset re-runs export only. The cache is opt-in with no default directory, and the ffmpeg, skill and contract versions are part of every key, so a cache is never reused across them. Audiogram (1.16). waveform.py --image cover.png (or render.py --template audiogram) puts the waveform over a still plate for an episode that has no picture, with --platform for the frame, --title and burnt-in captions. The image is a local file you give: nothing is fetched and no cover art is ever invented. Cut review. waveform.py clip.mp4 --at 12.4 --window 2 -o cut.png marks the chosen cut time on a waveform PNG. Repeat --at for numbered images and use the exported cut's own time coordinates when inspecting the edited file. Emoji in captions and titles (1.15). caption.py/graphics.py --emoji-assets DIR composites a PNG per emoji (Twemoji naming, 1f389.png, or Noto's emoji_u1f389.png) on top of the text, because drawtext cannot load a colour emoji font at all and an installed one does not prove libass will draw it in colour — doctor --json's fonts.emoji answers that from a render probe. Without assets the result's emoji.mode says which of three things happened: color when this build's libass draws the colour glyph (also for --emoji mono on such a build, with a warning), mono when it draws a monochrome one, and none when the emoji are left out of the text: with an emoji_not_drawn warning when that happened because nothing here draws the glyph, and with only an info line when --emoji none asked for it (and a graphics.py title that is nothing but emoji is refused). Nothing is ever downloaded. Indic and Thai text shaped correctly in titles and lower-thirds (1.15). graphics.py renders Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Thai and Lao through libass automatically (text_renderer: "ass"), because drawtext never reorders matras or re-clusters marks; Arabic and Hebrew were already correct on a fribidi build. --text-render drawtext with such a script is refused, never rendered wrongly. Non-Latin text picks a font by script (1.12). Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, Cyrillic and Greek cues, titles and overlays resolve a font file that covers them automatically, and a machine with no such font fails the job (kind: input) instead of rendering boxes. doctor --json's fonts.scripts says which languages this machine can render; --lang ja|ko disambiguates Han-only text, and --lang zh-TW (or zh-HK, zh-Hant) picks a Traditional Chinese face (2.19); an explicit --font/--font-file is always kept. Silence detection finds nothing? The default threshold is −35 dBFS. The tool prints a hint with the track's measured level; raise the threshold (silence.py --threshold -25) or shorten --min-silence. Sync results carry a confidence. Below 0.3, or an offset near the edge of the analysis window, is probably wrong: enlarge --analyze-seconds or find a clap. Recordings over ten minutes from separate devices need sync.py --fix-drift. Odd file names and unusable inputs are named, not passed to ffmpeg. A still called a%20b.png or logo%d.png is read as that one file; a relative subtitle, LUT or font path with a colon works (--srt ./a:b.srt); an input whose name starts with - is read as a file (give it after -- or as ./-name.mp4). An input that is empty, a directory, not media or not readable by the user is refused with its own error.reason (input_empty, input_is_directory, input_not_media, input_permission_denied) and a hint; an output extension this FFmpeg build has no muxer for (out.xyz) is refused before anything runs (output_extension_unknown), dry runs included. Outputs are never overwritten silently. An existing output path is refused (kind: input, error.reason: output_exists, before anything runs); pass --overwrite where a replacement is intended. Nothing happens silently. A refusal names its error.reason and error.details; a stale output lock taken over, a run without a lock, a plan input nobody could fingerprint, a fallback (an odd-sized frame scaled to even, a substituted font, libaom for SVT-AV1), a skipped step and every warning are recorded in diagnostics and on stderr (codes: json_output.diagnostic_codes); tools that draw text name the font face they drew with (font_used; libass draws a glyph that face lacks from another, not named). A refused plan and a lock takeover also append a line to an audit log (.audit.jsonl, or render.py --audit-log FILE). A degraded or partial result says so: render.py's verified is every stage's, an unmeasured loudness or a report section that could not be built is a failing verification step, export.py reports trimmed, multicam.py's cuts name the camera rendered, and batch.py rows carry the failing step's error, verified, and a row for every input after Ctrl-C. Long masters need a longer --timeout. The default is 1800 s per ffmpeg call, which is there to catch a hang. A full re-encode of an hour of 1080p at the default preset ran past it on a 4-core machine (see A one-hour recording). Pass --timeout 0 or a larger value, or --fast. Analysis and stream-copy cuts are far below it. Long chains belong in a plan. Three hand-chained re-encodes lose quality and are hard to change; render.py runs the whole edit from one JSON file, and --dry-run shows every ffmpeg command before anything is written. FAQ Can I pass raw ffmpeg arguments, or a filter_complex? Each operation is a script whose flags are its argparse parser, and that parser is what contract --json and the MCP inputSchema are built from. CI fails the build when those drift from the scripts. A caller-supplied filter graph, -vf string, or other ffmpeg option is not an argument any script accepts. doctor reads ffmpeg -filters (and -encoders, -bsfs) and reports a filter a tool needs before a job runs into it. MCP does accept an argv array, and that array is the named script's own CLI flags, still bound to that script: the script's flags, never an ffmpeg command line and never a shell. What if I need an option no tool exposes? For immediate use, run FFmpeg directly outside the skill. To request support in the skill, open an issue with the FFmpeg option, the kind of footage it applies to, and the result you need. New options are added as typed flags with tests and appear in the CLI and MCP schemas through the same contract. Why 42 tools? Isn't that overkill? One tool per job, because each job promises something different, and the tool measures that promise after the run. loudness.py re-measures integrated loudness and true peak. cut.py reports how far a cut snapped to a keyframe. silence.py returns the ranges it kept. export.py checks the preset's maximum length. A value a tool cannot read fails that step as not_measured; it does not pass. One tool with a mode flag would need as large a schema, and its checks would be vaguer. An agent does not read 42 schemas. Over MCP, tools/list advertises the core 12 (bold below). The other 30 are called by name through tools/call when a job needs one, and FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1 lists all 42. The groups are the ones in Tools. Group MCP default / all Tools Analysis and inspection 2 / 3 probe, look, scenes Editing 3 / 24 cut, fit, silence, join, crop, cropdetect, deinterlace, denoise, redact, sphere, straighten, insert, background, reverse, stabilize, sequence, waveform, freeze, pad, speedramp, loop, broll, metadata, grid Audio 2 / 3 audio, loudness, sync Picture 2 / 4 caption, graphics, overlay, color Delivery 2 / 4 export, check, proxy, report Orchestration 1 / 4 render, batch, multicam, verify Total 12 / 42 Without the other 30, an agent writes raw ffmpeg for those jobs, and a mistake there often still exits 0: stabilize.py runs vidstab in two passes, and the second pass needs the first pass's transforms file. color.py builds the HDR-to-SDR chain. With a wrong colour tag the run still finishes, and the picture comes out washed out. join.py puts transitions between clips that differ in size, frame rate or audio layout. Done by hand, those clips have to be normalised first or xfade fails. sync.py and multicam.py find the offset between two recordings by audio cross-correlation. No ffmpeg filter measures it. Every command a tool records as run is in its --json commands (batch.py lists none of its steps' commands, and a measurement pass is listed only where the tool records it), shell-quoted so it can be pasted and run again, except a line that names a file the tool wrote for the run and removed when it exited (such as a concat list, an ffmetadata file, a drawtext text file, a two-pass log or a stage's intermediate), and --dry-run on a writing tool prints the commands without writing the output (some dry runs still run a measurement, and verify.py ignores --dry-run: see below). In the 100-prompt agent eval (1.17.0, Tested on real footage) the agent made no raw ffmpeg calls and reported no false successes. What does verified check, and what can it not tell me? verified covers what can be measured from the file. Each tool measures its output again: the probe (the file opens, its duration, codecs, size and frame rate) and the tool's own promise. For example, loudness and true peak after loudness.py or export.py, the length against the asked one, and for cut.py, join.py and export.py the stream count, where picture and sound end, and whether both ends of every stream decode. check.py grades a file against a platform's limits. A value that cannot be read fails its step as not_measured; it does not pass. It cannot tell you whether the result looks or sounds right, and the result says so: every writing tool lists the properties it did not measure in unverified. Examples are picture_content (what is in the frame), subject_framing after a reframe, rendered_placement and legibility of captions and titles, grade_look after a colour conversion, removed_span_content after a silence cut (whether a removed span held speech), mix_balance and lip_sync. For those, look at frames with look.py (a contact sheet, or --safe for a platform's UI zones) and listen where the result points you. silence.py lists the level at every cut, and cut_warnings names the cuts that may have landed in a breath or a word's tail. For a single-file video delivery other than GIF, the call fails if an expected picture or audio stream is missing, the video codec (for an editing master also its profile and pixel format), dimensions or fixed frame rate differ from the preset, or the output exceeds a duration or file size limit. The written file stays available for diagnosis. When a platform preset specifies loudness, a failed loudness check marks the export unverified so the caller can decide whether to normalize or retry. check.py --content looks for black frames, freezes, flashes, silence and audio dropouts where the relevant stream exists. Review WARN rows for checks that could not measure a property. Delivery templates run these checks on the written file by default. A single-template render includes the rows in check.checks when it reaches the check stage. A dry run records check_dry_run and leaves check null. A real check adds decode time. For an intentional exception, fill the template with --write-project and set "check": {"platform": "...", "content": false} in the project before rendering. After a failed check, choose a new output or pass --overwrite to intentionally replace the retained file. JSON commands records the render's FFmpeg command lines. A single-template render lists content-check commands in check.commands. A social pack reports a verdict per output. Run check.py FILE --platform NAME --content on an individual file for its full rows and commands. For separate recordings, sync.py measures audio offset. Use --fix-drift to also request a drift measurement, which may be unavailable for short or low-confidence recordings. Review lip sync by watching and listening to the delivered file. When a real export fits video into a preset frame, picture gives the rectangle for pad, blur fill or crop if the measurement succeeds. If it fails, the report carries measured: false and a reason. How does ffmpeg-skill compare with Remotion? ffmpeg-skill edits footage you already have, on this machine, with FFmpeg tools whose flags are a machine-readable contract (contract --json). Remotion renders a video from React components. They complement each other: this repository does not call Remotion, and a file Remotion writes is an ordinary input (probe.py, cut.py, fit.py, export.py, check.py). remotion-ffmpeg-skill joins the two. It measures the footage with this repo, draws the graphics in Remotion from those measurements, and checks and delivers the result with this repo again. Install both (npx ffmpeg-skill, then npx remotion-ffmpeg-skill). As with the other skills, the dependency runs one way: it calls these tools, and nothing here calls it. HyperFrames renders a video from HTML and is the same kind of neighbour: a file it writes is an ordinary input too. Does it validate the filter graph before running? No. --dry-run prints the ffmpeg command a writing tool would run and does not start ffmpeg, so ffmpeg never parses that filter graph. ffprobe still runs when the tool probes an input that exists. Unless --overwrite is passed, an existing output is refused (kind: input) before ffmpeg. An output that is the same file as an input is refused either way. No media file is written, and verified is false; --plan FILE does write the plan JSON. A path that is not on disk yet is not measured: the probe is a stub (0×0, duration 0), so a number taken from it is not a measurement. A plan is not a promise of the outcome: cut.py's plan of a stream copy names in possible_reencode_reason what a real run may still re-encode it for (tolerance: where the copy lands is measured from the written file). A real render.py run starts with its own dry run, so when that dry run is refused because a stage needs a filter or an encoder the build lacks, the real run is refused the same way before the first stage encodes. The measuring tools (probe, check, sync, multicam, scenes, cropdetect, report, silence, loudness, stabilize) still run their measurements; only the artifact is skipped, and silence with --transcribe (with --filler or a sentence flag) also runs the speech engine, which may download a model. overlay measures the lines of a multi-line --text with one drawtext on a generated frame on FFmpeg 8.0, 8.0.1 and 8.1.0, where it draws them one by one. metadata with --auto-chapters and cut with --snap beats decode the input for their measurement, and render and batch run each stage or step as its own dry run, so a measuring stage measures an input that exists; a stage or an item a real run would serve from its cache is not run, as the real run does not run it (render's cache.would_hit; batch's row cached: true, with what the run that stored it measured and verified). verify accepts --dry-run and ignores it: its steps run, and its document says dry_run: false. --plan FILE is that dry run written down — the planned argv, the command lines, and a fingerprint of each existing input (size, plus a sha256 of the first and last 8 MiB). render.py and verify.py refuse --plan. render.py FILE runs a plan only when those fingerprints still match (a mismatch is refused with each input's expected and actual fingerprint in error.details, and logged to .audit.jsonl), by running the tool again with the planned argv, not by executing the recorded ffmpeg lines; --dry-run on that run only prints them. doctor reports whether the filters, encoders and bitstream filters the contract names are in this build (ffmpeg -filters, -encoders, -bsfs) and which fonts are installed. A name in that listing is not a check of the graph this command would build, and a listed GPU encoder is not a successful encode. Can it remove burned-in subtitles or logos? A rectangle you already know, sitting still for the whole clip, can be filled from the picture around it with redact.py --mode delogo (ffmpeg's delogo filter). That is a 1 px border blend. It is not inpainting: a logo that moves, or burned-in subtitles whose position changes, is out of scope. The same known box can be obscured instead, with --mode blur or --mode pixelate. None of the three finds the box. delogo also needs the box at least 1 px inside the frame, and it only interpolates 8-bit YUV, so an HDR or 10-bit source is refused until color.py --to-sdr. Does it auto-track faces or subjects for reframing? fit.py --fit crop centres the crop unless you pass --crop-x and --crop-y. Use look.py OUTPUT --at TIME with an indicated output_time_estimate to inspect one. crop.py cuts the rectangle you pass. cropdetect.py --motion-centre reports where motion sat each second. sphere.py points a 360 view where you aim it. Subject framing still needs visual review. Does it encode on the GPU? The encode path a tool will actually take is Apple VideoToolbox, for h264, hevc and prores, and only on Apple Silicon. --hw asks for it on that call. FFMPEG_SKILL_HW=1 makes it the default for every re-encoding tool except export.py's delivery presets, which take --hw on their own (or render.py --hw for a whole project). AV1 stays on SVT-AV1. nvenc, QSV, VAAPI and AMF are reported by doctor --json's gpu_encoders when the ffmpeg build was compiled with them, and no tool encodes with them. One build is the exception to opt-in: with no libx264 and no libx265, and with h264_videotoolbox or hevc_videotoolbox, those encodes use VideoToolbox without --hw and the result says hw.source is "auto". --no-hw still asks for the CPU encoder. A VideoToolbox job the hardware refuses is re-encoded on the CPU and the result says so (hw.fallback). Releasing is fully automated end to end, including the version number itself — a PR never needs to touch package.json or the version in docs/contract.md. CHANGELOG.md is different: the release writes the version heading and one line per merged PR, but a feat PR writes its own notes under ## Unreleased (CONTRIBUTING.md), and a PR that closes an issue must name that issue in CHANGELOG.md or test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag fails. Once a PR merges to main, .github/workflows/release.yml takes it from there: if nobody bumped the version by hand, it resolves the next version with .github/scripts/resolve_version.py. What that script reads, its rules, their exceptions and the incidents behind them are written once, in its docstring, and test_release_version_resolver_rules and test_release_version_resolver_does_not_depend_on_a_pr_title pin them; they are not restated here. Most PRs don't need a label added by hand: release-drafter.yml's autolabel job applies one automatically from the PR's title/changed files (Fix ... → fix, Add .../feat ... → feature, docs/.md/.github//build(deps) changes → chore) as soon as it's opened — add a label yourself only to override that. A major version is never chosen automatically: no label rule produces major, and the workflow refuses to auto-bump across a major boundary even if someone applies that label — a real major release is a deliberate package.json bump in a PR, which the manual path below already handles. It bumps package.json, .claude-plugin/plugin.json, docs/contract.md and docs/roadmap.md's released-version sentence, writes a CHANGELOG.md section listing those PRs (and any issues they closed), and pushes that commit to main itself. If another PR merged while the bump was being prepared, the push is refused and that run releases nothing: the newer merge's own run, queued behind it, starts from main's tip and releases both (the bump is never rebased onto a merge it did not read). After the tag it also asks pages.yml to rebuild the site, because the bump commit carries [skip ci] and would otherwise leave the site on the previous version. Either way — auto-bumped or hand-bumped in the PR — it then creates the vX.Y.Z tag, publishes a GitHub Release with notes extracted from CHANGELOG.md's matching section, and publishes the package to npm. A PR that still wants to write its own version bump and CHANGELOG.md prose (e.g. to explain the "why" of a release by hand) can — the automation only fills in when nobody made that call already. A push to main with nothing new to release creates no tag, Release or npm publish; its MCP Registry step still asks npm and the registry about server.json's version and publishes the entry only when npm has that version and the registry does not, which is how a later run finishes an entry an earlier one failed to publish. npm publishing needs an NPM_TOKEN repo secret (an npm access token with publish rights on this package) — without it the tag and GitHub Release still happen, only the npm step is skipped. A repo that depends on this one (an editing skill, an agent) should pin an ffmpeg-skill version by tag or npm version, not by tracking main — a merged-but-not-yet-released commit on main can be ahead of the last published npm version for the few minutes between merge and this workflow completing. A version that was tagged but never reached npm (the npm step failed; a re-run of that release sees the tag and skips the publish) is finished by dispatching the same workflow on its tag: gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f version=X.Y.Z. That runs only the workflow's recover job. It refuses a version that is not X.Y.Z, has no tag, or that npm already has, and a run whose commit is not the tagged one: the npm provenance attestation names the run's commit, so it must be the commit the package is built from. It publishes with --provenance under the latest dist-tag when the version is above every stable (non-prerelease) version npm has, and under backport otherwise, so latest never moves back. Then it publishes the plugin branch when no commit there is for this version and the branch's tip is older, and the MCP Registry entry when the registry does not list the version (never for a backport). The GitHub Release is left as it is. A tag cut before the job was added (#448; every tag up to v3.6.3) has no recover job at its commit and cannot be recovered this way.
